questions.text: Who is named as the owner of this plan (shown in its header)?
questions.why: The plan of record names an accountable owner; the header and sign-off use it.
options: You, by the name you give
A team name you give
questions.recommend: You, by the name you give|You commissioned it and sign it off
questions.answer: Owner: ChristopherLinnett (the user).

questions.text: Is this an official ArtCraft Team project, or an independent SDK built on EffectCraft? The ArtCraft brand licence forbids the ArtCraft name or marks in the name, listing or marketing of anything other than EffectCraft itself without the ArtCraft Team's written permission.
questions.why: Decides the published package names (Swift module, Maven coordinates, repo name) and what the README may say; an unlicensed 'ArtCraft …' name would have to be renamed after release.
options: Independent: neutral product name, README says 'based on EffectCraft by the ArtCraft team'
Official: ArtCraft Team gives written permission and the SDK may carry the ArtCraft name
questions.recommend: Independent: neutral product name, README says 'based on EffectCraft by the ArtCraft team'|Needs no permission to start; can be renamed into an official package later if the team adopts it
questions.answer: Independent SDK: a neutral product name, and the README says in plain text that it is based on EffectCraft by the ArtCraft team; no ArtCraft name or marks in names, listings or marketing.

questions.text: Where does the plugin code live, under which licence, and where are the built packages published?
questions.why: Fixes the repository the build steps create, the licence headers, and the release targets the packaging steps publish to (SwiftPM binary URL, Maven repository).
options: A new repo under your personal GitHub account, MIT OR Apache-2.0 like EffectCraft, releases on GitHub Releases (XCFramework zip for SwiftPM) and GitHub Packages (Maven AAR)
The same, but private until a first release
Local only for now: build and consume packages from disk, publishing decided later
questions.recommend: The same, but private until a first release|Lets the build run end to end, including release automation, without publishing anything before you decide
questions.answer: A new repository under the ChristopherLinnett GitHub account, licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0, private until a first release; releases on GitHub Releases (XCFramework zip for SwiftPM) and GitHub Packages (Maven AAR).

questions.text: How do the plugins stay linked to EffectCraft (RQ4)?
questions.why: Decides the repository layout, the update procedure and how deterministic an upstream update is; it shapes Part B and every build step.
options: Depend on the unmodified upstream crates at a pinned git revision; generate the Swift and Kotlin API from the engine's own command registry and tool catalogue; one update script bumps the pin, regenerates, diffs the API surface and runs the conformance suite
Fork storytold/effectcraft and add the mobile crates inside the fork, merging upstream periodically
Propose the mobile crates into storytold/effectcraft itself
questions.recommend: Depend on the unmodified upstream crates at a pinned git revision; generate the Swift and Kotlin API from the engine's own command registry and tool catalogue; one update script bumps the pin, regenerates, diffs the API surface and runs the conformance suite|No fork to keep merging, and an update is a pin bump plus regeneration. Upstream forbids unsafe code workspace-wide, and an FFI layer needs it, so the mobile crates cannot live inside the upstream workspace without a rule exception
questions.answer: The plugins depend on the unmodified upstream crates at a pinned git revision; the Swift and Kotlin API is generated from the engine's command registry and tool catalogue; one update script bumps the pin, regenerates, diffs the API surface and runs the conformance suite.

questions.text: May the build contribute small seams to storytold/effectcraft as pull requests (through your fork), where the plugins would otherwise copy upstream code or work around it?
questions.why: Without them the plugin must set process environment variables at start-up (config, cache and font folders), cannot find system fonts on iOS or Android, and cannot use hardware video encoders without re-implementing the export pipeline; each workaround is code that drifts from upstream.
options: Yes: plan them as upstream PRs, with a plugin-side fallback until each merges
No: the plugin works around them and never depends on upstream changes
questions.recommend: Yes: plan them as upstream PRs, with a plugin-side fallback until each merges|Keeps one source of truth upstream; the fallbacks mean the plugin never waits on a merge
questions.answer: Yes: small seams are proposed to storytold/effectcraft as pull requests through the ChristopherLinnett fork, each with a plugin-side fallback until it merges.

questions.text: Which EffectCraft CLI capabilities must the first release expose as device APIs (RQ2)?
questions.why: Sets the API surface, the conformance suite and the size of the build. The CLI's bridge mode drives a desktop app over a local TCP port, and its operations and Roto Brush benchmarks depend on the desktop UI and on installed models.
options: Everything except --bridge and the UI/Roto benchmarks: info, commands, exec, run, props, get, set, render-frame, render (every format, --queue, templates), script, replay, an in-process MCP endpoint, and render timings
Literally everything, including bridge mode to a desktop app on the network and every benchmark
Core only: exec, run, props, get, set, render-frame, render
questions.recommend: Everything except --bridge and the UI/Roto benchmarks: info, commands, exec, run, props, get, set, render-frame, render (every format, --queue, templates), script, replay, an in-process MCP endpoint, and render timings|Covers every document operation the CLI can perform; bridge mode and the UI benchmarks exist to drive or measure the desktop app, which a phone does not run
questions.answer: Everything except --bridge and the UI/Roto benchmarks: info, commands, exec, run, props, get, set, render-frame, render (every format, --queue, templates), script, replay, an in-process MCP endpoint, and render timings.

questions.text: What shape should the Swift and Kotlin APIs take?
questions.why: Decides what the code generator emits, what the docs show developers, and how much hand-written API has to be maintained when upstream changes.
options: Two layers: a generated typed facade (one method per engine command with named parameters, regenerated on every update) plus a generic exec(id, params) / run(steps); hand-written typed calls only for the fixed-shape operations (render, props, get, set, templates)
Generic only: exec(id, JSON) and run(steps), developers read the command list
Hand-written typed API for every command
questions.recommend: Two layers: a generated typed facade (one method per engine command with named parameters, regenerated on every update) plus a generic exec(id, params) / run(steps); hand-written typed calls only for the fixed-shape operations (render, props, get, set, templates)|The engine registers 763 commands; their parameter docs give names and optionality in a machine-readable form, and types only as prose hints (bool, enum lists, [x,y], seconds); generating them keeps updates mechanical, and the hand-written part stays small
questions.answer: Two layers: a generated typed facade (one method per engine command with named parameters, regenerated on every update) plus a generic exec(id, params) / run(steps); hand-written typed calls only for the fixed-shape operations (render, props, get, set, templates).

questions.text: How should rendered frames reach the developer's interface?
questions.why: Decides whether the SDK owns on-screen drawing paths (CAMetalLayer on iOS, Surface on Android) and whether frames ever leave the GPU; affects performance, battery and the API.
options: Three outputs: render into a layer or surface the developer passes in (frames stay on the GPU), a platform image (CVPixelBuffer / Android Bitmap or HardwareBuffer), and encoded PNG bytes; no UI widgets
Images and PNG bytes only
The three outputs plus ready-made SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose preview views
questions.recommend: Three outputs: render into a layer or surface the developer passes in (frames stay on the GPU), a platform image (CVPixelBuffer / Android Bitmap or HardwareBuffer), and encoded PNG bytes; no UI widgets|You said developers connect their own interface; drawing into their layer is the native, zero-copy way to show a live preview
questions.answer: Three outputs: render into a layer or surface the developer passes in (frames stay on the GPU), a platform image (CVPixelBuffer / Android Bitmap or HardwareBuffer), and encoded PNG bytes; no UI widgets.

questions.text: Should the first build split the work into a universal Craft core plugin plus an EffectCraft plugin, or build an EffectCraft-only plugin and extract the core when a second app arrives (RQ8)?
questions.why: Decides the package and crate layout every build step creates, and whether a second Craft app later imports the core or forces a refactor of the EffectCraft plugin.
options: Two layers from the start: a universal core (Rust crate + Swift package + Kotlin library: request channel, progress and cancellation, errors, GPU device, folders, fonts, native video decoding) that knows nothing of EffectCraft, plus the EffectCraft plugin that imports it; the core holds only what EffectCraft needs today
EffectCraft-only first; extract the core when FilmCraft or FigCraft gets a plugin
questions.recommend: Two layers from the start: a universal core (Rust crate + Swift package + Kotlin library: request channel, progress and cancellation, errors, GPU device, folders, fonts, native video decoding) that knows nothing of EffectCraft, plus the EffectCraft plugin that imports it; the core holds only what EffectCraft needs today|EffectCraft, FilmCraft and FigCraft share the registry, session and control-protocol shape, and craft-web-api already shares the web equivalent the same way; splitting now costs a crate boundary, splitting later means moving code out of a shipped package
questions.answer: Two layers from the start: a universal core that knows nothing of EffectCraft (request channel, progress and cancellation, errors, GPU device, folders, fonts, native video decoding) plus the EffectCraft plugin that imports it; the core holds only what EffectCraft needs today.

questions.text: Where should the universal core live?
questions.why: Decides which repository the core's crates and packages are created in, who can change them, and whether other Craft app plugins can depend on it without depending on the EffectCraft plugin.
options: In the plugin-port repository as its own crate and packages (artcraft-plugin-port/core), next to effectcraft/; propose it to storytold/craft-libs later if the maintainers want it
Propose it to storytold/craft-libs now, as a new shared crate
A separate repository of its own
questions.recommend: In the plugin-port repository as its own crate and packages (artcraft-plugin-port/core), next to effectcraft/; propose it to storytold/craft-libs later if the maintainers want it|No dependency on maintainers' review to start; the folder layout you described (artcraft-plugin-port/<app>) gains one sibling, and moving a self-contained crate to craft-libs later is a path change
questions.answer: The universal core lives in the plugin-port repository as its own crate and packages (artcraft-plugin-port/core, next to effectcraft/).

questions.text: Which minimum OS versions and CPU architectures should the plugins support?
questions.why: Sets the Xcode deployment target, Android minSdk, the ABIs built and tested, and which GPU paths can be assumed. Devices without Metal or Vulkan compute still work on the CPU path.
options: iOS 17+ (arm64 device, arm64 simulator); Android 10+ (API 29), arm64-v8a plus x86_64 for emulators, no 32-bit
iOS 16+; Android 8.0+ (API 26), arm64-v8a, x86_64 and armeabi-v7a
iOS 18+ (as storytold/effectcraft#1401 chose); Android 13+ (API 33), arm64-v8a only
questions.recommend: iOS 17+ (arm64 device, arm64 simulator); Android 10+ (API 29), arm64-v8a plus x86_64 for emulators, no 32-bit|A product judgement, not measured market share: Android 10 is where apps lose the right to run their own binaries and launch devices must offer Vulkan 1.1; 32-bit Android was not built or tested in the feasibility runs
questions.answer: iOS 17+ (arm64 device, arm64 simulator); Android 10+ (API 29), arm64-v8a plus x86_64 for emulators, no 32-bit.

questions.text: How should the plugins decode and encode video: through the platform's hardware codecs or EffectCraft's own pure-Rust codecs (RQ3)?
questions.why: Decides battery and speed for footage-heavy projects, whether exports match the desktop's output, and which upstream changes the build depends on. EffectCraft's maintainers keep OS codec code out of their own binary (storytold/effectcraft#819); a plugin is a separate product and may include it.
options: Hybrid: decode H.264 and HEVC (and AV1 where the device has it) with VideoToolbox on iOS and MediaCodec on Android, registered in front of the pure-Rust decoders, which remain the fallback; encode with the pure-Rust encoders until an encoder seam exists upstream, then add hardware H.264/HEVC encoding as an export option
Pure-Rust only: identical behaviour to the desktop, no platform codec code
Hardware both ways from the first release, which first requires the upstream encoder seam
questions.recommend: Hybrid: decode H.264 and HEVC (and AV1 where the device has it) with VideoToolbox on iOS and MediaCodec on Android, registered in front of the pure-Rust decoders, which remain the fallback; encode with the pure-Rust encoders until an encoder seam exists upstream, then add hardware H.264/HEVC encoding as an export option|Hardware decoding plugs into FilmCraft's decoder registry with no EffectCraft change and was measured bit-exact on desktop; hardware encoding needs an upstream seam the plugin cannot add alone
questions.answer: Hybrid: H.264 and HEVC (and AV1 where the device has it) decode through VideoToolbox on iOS and MediaCodec on Android, registered in front of the pure-Rust decoders, which remain the fallback; exports use the pure-Rust encoders until an encoder seam exists upstream, then hardware H.264/HEVC encoding becomes an export option.

questions.text: Should the plugins run JavaScript (scripts and expressions) and load WebAssembly effect plug-ins on device?
questions.why: Scripts and expressions are part of what the CLI does (script, expressions in projects). Apple allows a bundled interpreter running user-written scripts; whether downloaded WebAssembly plug-ins count as interpreted code is not addressed by Apple's rules. External helper effects are separate processes, which neither iOS nor Android allows, so they are unavailable either way.
options: Scripts and expressions on both platforms; WebAssembly plug-ins on Android always, on iOS only from files the host app bundles, with a switch the host app can turn off
Scripts, expressions and WebAssembly plug-ins on both platforms; the host app decides what to allow
Scripts and expressions only; no WebAssembly plug-ins on either platform
questions.recommend: Scripts and expressions on both platforms; WebAssembly plug-ins on Android always, on iOS only from files the host app bundles, with a switch the host app can turn off|Keeps full document parity (projects with expressions render the same) while leaving the App Review judgement on downloaded plug-ins with the host app
questions.answer: Scripts and expressions run on both platforms; WebAssembly plug-ins load on Android always and on iOS only from files the host app bundles, behind a switch the host app can turn off.

questions.text: Who schedules long exports when the user leaves the app?
questions.why: iOS stops GPU work in the background unless the app runs a BGContinuedProcessingTask with a GPU entitlement; Android needs a mediaProcessing foreground service. Whoever owns this needs the entitlement, the permission and the system progress UI.
options: The host app: the SDK exposes progress, cancellation and a background-safe export call, documents the iOS and Android recipes, and ships a sample of each
The SDK starts and manages the background task and foreground service itself
Out of scope: exports run only while the app is in the foreground
questions.recommend: The host app: the SDK exposes progress, cancellation and a background-safe export call, documents the iOS and Android recipes, and ships a sample of each|Entitlements, permissions and the system progress UI belong to the app's identity and review; an SDK that starts them would impose them on every host app
questions.answer: The host app schedules background exports; the SDK exposes progress, cancellation and a background-safe export call, documents the iOS and Android recipes and ships a sample of each.

questions.text: Is an engine library of about 60 MB per architecture acceptable for the first release?
questions.why: The release Android build of the engine is 62.4 MB stripped (26.7 MB compressed). Everything the CLI does includes PSD, AEP, PDF, SVG, Lottie, 3D models, SAM 2 and every codec, which the engine links unconditionally; making them optional needs upstream feature flags.
options: Yes for the first release; measure the plugin library itself and report its size with each release
No: the first release ships optional modules, which requires upstream feature flags before the build can finish
Set a budget now (you name it) and the plan finds what to cut
questions.recommend: Yes for the first release; measure the plugin library itself and report its size with each release|Full CLI parity is the requirement, and every module the engine links is part of it; trimming needs upstream changes the first release should not wait for
questions.answer: An engine library of about 60 MB per architecture is acceptable for the first release; the plugin library's own size is measured and reported with each release.

questions.text: What are the SDK's product and package names? (PD2 rules out the ArtCraft name; the brand licence names only the ArtCraft name and marks, not 'EffectCraft', but forbids presenting a derived work as an ArtCraft product.)
questions.why: Fixes the GitHub repository name, the Rust crate names, the Swift package and module names and the Maven coordinates that every build step creates; renaming after a release breaks every integrating app.
options: CraftBridge: repo ChristopherLinnett/craftbridge; core CraftBridge (Swift) / io.github.christopherlinnett.craftbridge:core (Maven); EffectCraft plugin CraftBridgeEffects / io.github.christopherlinnett.craftbridge:effects
EffectCraftKit: core CraftKit, EffectCraft plugin EffectCraftKit, which names the engine plainly but may read as an official EffectCraft product
A name you choose
questions.recommend: CraftBridge: repo ChristopherLinnett/craftbridge; core CraftBridge (Swift) / io.github.christopherlinnett.craftbridge:core (Maven); EffectCraft plugin CraftBridgeEffects / io.github.christopherlinnett.craftbridge:effects|Says what it is (a bridge from Swift and Kotlin to the Craft engines) without the ArtCraft name, and leaves room for CraftBridgeFilm and the rest; the local folder artcraft-plugin-port stays as it is
questions.answer: CraftBridge: repository ChristopherLinnett/craftbridge; the universal core is CraftBridge (Swift) and io.github.christopherlinnett.craftbridge:core (Maven); the EffectCraft plugin is CraftBridgeEffects and io.github.christopherlinnett.craftbridge:effects; the local folder artcraft-plugin-port stays as it is.

questions.text: Native video decoders: extend FilmCraft's filmcraft-platform (which already has the macOS VideoToolbox decoder) through a new ChristopherLinnett/filmcraft fork and pull requests to storytold/filmcraft, or write CraftBridge's own decoders?
questions.why: PD12 needs VideoToolbox (iOS) and MediaCodec (Android) decoders. FilmCraft's decoder compiles for iOS with three gate changes (tested); a second implementation in CraftBridge would duplicate it. Extending FilmCraft means creating a fork of storytold/filmcraft under ChristopherLinnett.
options: Extend filmcraft-platform: fork storytold/filmcraft, propose the iOS gates and a MediaCodec decoder as pull requests, and pin CraftBridge to the fork commit on EffectCraft's FilmCraft revision through a Cargo patch until FilmCraft merges them and EffectCraft's pin includes them
Write VideoToolbox and MediaCodec decoders in CraftBridge's core, registered through FilmCraft's public decoder registry; no fork
questions.recommend: Extend filmcraft-platform: fork storytold/filmcraft, propose the iOS gates and a MediaCodec decoder as pull requests, and pin CraftBridge to the fork commit on EffectCraft's FilmCraft revision through a Cargo patch until FilmCraft merges them and EffectCraft's pin includes them|One VideoToolbox decoder for the whole suite, extended rather than copied
questions.answer: CraftBridge's own decoders: the universal core carries the VideoToolbox (iOS) and MediaCodec (Android) hardware decoders, registered through FilmCraft's public decoder registry that EffectCraft already decodes through; every app plugin (CraftBridgeEffects now, CraftBridgeFilm later) imports them from the core; no FilmCraft fork and no FilmCraft pull requests.

questions.text: PD5's plugin-side fallback for seams whose code lives only in the EffectCraft CLI binary (template rendering, render timings): until each seam pull request merges, should CraftBridge build against your fork's pull-request branch (the upstream pin plus that PR's commits), instead of carrying a copy of the CLI code?
questions.why: Template rendering (190 lines) and render timings exist only in the CLI binary, so the plugin can reuse them only from a library. A copy would drift from upstream; the pull-request branch keeps one source and is replaced by the upstream pin once merged.
options: Yes: pin the fork's PR branch until merged; the update script rebases it onto each new upstream pin
No: those capabilities ship only after their PRs merge upstream
questions.recommend: Yes: pin the fork's PR branch until merged; the update script rebases it onto each new upstream pin|Every PD6 capability ships in the first release without a copied line of upstream code
questions.answer: Until a seam pull request merges upstream, CraftBridge builds against the ChristopherLinnett/effectcraft pull-request branch (the upstream pin plus that PR's commits) rather than a copy of CLI code; the update script rebases the branch onto each new upstream pin, and the pin returns to storytold/effectcraft once the PR merges.

questions.text: How is the CraftBridge repository laid out?
questions.why: Every path in §15, §20–§25, §31 and Appendix A follows from it
options: one folder per platform, each a complete build
product folders, then language (core/, effectcraft/)
questions.recommend: one folder per platform|each toolchain's files stay in its own folder; nothing of a platform sits at the root
questions.answer: One folder per platform, each a complete build: rust/, ios/ and android/, with clean separation of the libraries; Package.swift sits at the top of the iOS section (ios/sdk) rather than the repository root, nesting a level deeper where that keeps the libraries separate, and releases reach SwiftPM by whatever best achieves that separation.

questions.text: When does the CraftBridge repository become public?
questions.why: Decides when hosted CI runs (free on public repositories) and what G3 still gates
options: when hosted CI starts
at the first release
questions.recommend: when hosted CI starts|hosted runners, macOS included, are free on public repositories
questions.answer: Private initially; the repository becomes public when hosted CI starts, so CI can run and validate there.
supersedes: stays private until the owner releases it

questions.text: Does CraftBridge change EffectCraft to support phones?
questions.why: Decides PD4, PD5, PD12 and PD17, §15's seams, wave W1 and how updates are taken
options: never: adapt inside CraftBridge
small seams proposed upstream
questions.recommend: never: adapt inside CraftBridge|a standalone project that follows official releases
questions.answer: We don't modify EffectCraft; we make the relevant changes in this project. If iOS or Android need a modified or adapted variant of something, including hardware encoding, it goes in this project. CraftBridge is a standalone project, built so that official EffectCraft updates are not painful to integrate (not necessarily automatic), not one that puts surgical changes into EffectCraft.
